If one extrapolates Einstein’s equations back to t = 0 a singularity appears—a point of infinite density and temperature—signalling that the theory ceases to be valid. Thus asking what happened prior to it is problematic.

testCases.input: How does inflation address the horizon and flatness problems?
testCases.actualOutput:
Inflation solves both problems by invoking an extremely rapid, exponential expansion of space in the first tiny fraction of a second after the Big Bang.  

* **Horizon problem:** Because the universe expands so dramatically (by at least a factor of 10^50 between about 10⁻³⁷ – 10⁻³⁴ seconds after the origin), a region that was once tiny and thermally connected is stretched far beyond the observable horizon. This means that the parts of the sky we now see as causally disconnected were actually in contact before inflation, allowing them to come to the same temperature and density.  

* **Flatness problem:** The same exponential stretching smooths out any initial curvature of space. As space expands enormously, any deviation from perfect flatness is driven toward zero, leaving the large‑scale universe geometrically flat, as observed.  

Thus, inflation’s brief but immense expansion both homogenizes the observable universe and flattens its geometry, directly addressing the horizon and flatness problems.

This expansion stretches a previously small, causally connected region to a much larger scale, explaining observed large-scale uniformity while driving spatial geometry toward near-flatness.

The inflationary model posits that around 10^-36 seconds (a billionth of a billionth of a billionth of a second) after the Big Bang, the universe underwent an extremely rapid, exponential expansion. This idea was proposed to explain why the universe appears so uniform on large scales (the horizon problem) and why space is nearly geometrically flat (the flatness problem). Inflation would have stretched any initial inhomogeneities to cosmic size and also magnified quantum fluctuations, seeding the galaxies and large-scale structures we see today

. Inflationary cosmology resolves these issues by positing that between 10^{-37} and 10^{-34} seconds after the origin, a scalar energy field drove an exponential expansion of space, increasing the size of the universe by a factor of at least 10^{50}. This rapid stretching smoothed out spatial curvature and expanded a tiny, thermally connected region far beyond the observable horizon. In many inflationary models, quantum fluctuations prevent the scalar field from decaying uniformly across all space. While inflation halts in localized pockets—forming individual "bubble universes" like our own—the surrounding space continues to expand exponentially. This process, known as eternal inflation, naturally generates a Level II Multiverse
